blocks.p: The Axis came up the way weather comes. Rei did not call it. It simply arrived.

It came up through the one register the two brothers shared. Under both their suppressions there was the same family grain, the Uedera grain. The far shore had found that shape in Rei's hand when it sent him into the tear, and it had keyed the two brothers to a single office. When Rei first felt the Axis, he had felt it as a balance point. A fulcrum is the small fixed point a seesaw rests on, the one point that lets both ends move. That was how it had felt to him, one living point with two suppressed registers leaning on it from either side. On the thin night he understood it differently. It was the only thing in the city that did not want either of them in the chair.

It rose up between the brothers and the wound, and it reached out in two directions at once. It reached for Rei's register. It reached for what was left of Gin's. Against every line of the Healer's arithmetic, it tried to keep both of them off the seat by holding both of them up.

For one impossible second it worked. The chair asked, and neither register answered, because the Axis was holding them both, balanced and hanging in the air. Two brothers were held an inch above the chair by the thing in them that would not let the other one fall.
In that second Rei saw it.

blocks.cap: The face at the centre of the light, there and gone

blocks.p: It was not a force. It was a face. It was there and gone at the centre of the light, the way a face appears in a window at night when the room behind the glass is lit. A young man, perhaps thirty, in a plain dark coat of a cut nobody had worn for a hundred and fifty years. His hair was tied back. His expression was calm and attentive and very tired. He looked at Rei the way a man looks at a word he once knew and loved and has lost the meaning of. His back was turned to everything else. His whole attention was on the wall.

Gin's book had described the Axis in its careful, clinical way, in the pages he could not prove. It answers one question per approach. It does not show its face. It returns the practitioner. In plain words, a person who reaches the Axis may ask it one thing, and then it pushes them back out. But now it was showing its face. It was not pushing anyone back. It was too busy holding two people up.

Rei had one question. He knew the rule. He did not ask how to save Gin, or which of them the chair would take, or how long the wall would hold. He asked the thing he had wanted to ask ever since the Axis had shoved him back into the world.
"What are you holding?"
The answer did not come in words. It came as the shape of an old word settling down inside him. The seat I became.

Rei kept it next to something else. In the kitchen, with the last of his clear strength, Gin had managed half a sentence. The chair doesn't need a new occupant. It needs its old one. Rei did not understand either of them yet. He knew he would.
Then the Axis began to stretch.

Rei felt something that Higuchi's smallest letters had never had room to say. The Axis was built to carry one. It was a balance point, not a bridge. It held the city level the way the thin edge under a pair of scales holds the scales level. Ask that edge to carry both pans at once and it does not balance. It bends. Rei felt it bend inside his chest. The register the brothers shared went tight and thin and bright, like the seam over the river. The two of them were held. But the thing holding them was paying for it in the only money it had, which was itself.

It had been paying already, Rei understood. Since 2009 it had carried the thirteenth seat directly from the centre, with no living holder to take any of the weight. An Axis that is stretched too far makes mistakes. The thinning Kita had suffered for six years was partly the sound of a man at the centre holding too much for too long.

The Healer watched this with an attention that was, for the first time all month, truly surprised. It had not planned for the Axis to refuse the chair. It had planned for the shared register to be the very thing that made one of the brothers fit the chair. Now that register was straining itself to pieces to keep both of them out of the seat the Healer had spent so long preparing. For the first time, Rei had made the trap do something it was not built to do.
The cost was that he could feel exactly how long the Axis could keep it up. Not long.

"Ah," the Healer said softly, in his brother's tired voice. The surprise in it slowly turned into something like respect. "You would do that. Of course you would. You would rather burn the fulcrum than let it choose. You would rather both of you fall than either of you sit, because to you the unbearable thing was never the open chair. It was being made to pick. I did account for your love, Rei. I built the whole engine on it. I did not account for your love taking this shape. The shape that would rather end the thing that connects you than let it hand down a verdict."
Across the water Kaito tilted his borrowed head. He looked interested, the way a cat is interested in a bird that has flown into a window.

The seam over the river answered the strain. It thinned faster. The two cities slid another degree apart, because the Axis was spending itself, and the wall felt that spending the way the holders feel everything, as weight pressing on a seam.

"But understand what you are doing," the Healer said. "The Axis is what has kept the wound honest. Stretch it to breaking and the chair does not close. It tears. There is no seat left to fill, only a hole, and a city does not survive an unmade office any better than a vacant one. You have found the one move I did not see. It is also the one move that ends with no door at all."
